completeSourceDiscovery.boundaryContinuationRule: a move beginning in lookbehind remains owned by the predecessor chunk

candidates.speaker: Michael Huemer
candidates.proposition: The maximal traditional conception of God is impossible because infinite power, knowledge, and intelligence are impossible non-extensive magnitudes.
candidates.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly assigns the opening presentation to Huemer, and the uninterrupted first-person argument continues until his concluding revision of the concept of God.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This is Huemer's principal case against the coherence of the stipulated maximal theism and directly supplies his reason for accepting only a finite deity.
candidates.contextSummary: After distinguishing his objection from familiar omnipotence and foreknowledge puzzles, Huemer develops a taxonomy meant to separate possible extensive infinities from impossible quantitative infinities.

candidates.speaker: Richard Swinburne
candidates.proposition: The impossibility of an infinite being does not undermine Christian theism because historically authoritative Christian formulations did not describe God as infinite in the disputed quantitative senses.
candidates.attributionBasis: The moderator hands the floor to Swinburne, whose marked response begins at event 349 and directly addresses Huemer's preceding presentation.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move attempts to defeat the central incoherence charge by denying that the allegedly impossible infinity belongs to the relevant Christian conception of God.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Huemer's claim that traditional theism requires a God with impossible infinite quantitative attributes.

candidates.contextSummary: Swinburne accepts much of Huemer's criticism of quantitative infinity but argues that it is irrelevant to historic Christian theism and proposes addressing other coherence objections.

candidates.speaker: Richard Swinburne
candidates.proposition: The coherent concept of God should be inferred from the most probable ultimate cause of the universe rather than tested as an isolated maximal definition.
candidates.attributionBasis: This argument continues within Swinburne's uninterrupted response and is signaled as his alternative way of approaching the issue.
candidates.loadBearingReason: It replaces Huemer's definitional starting point with an abductive methodology under which an everlasting omnipotent source is inferred from general features of reality.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Huemer's method of assessing coherence by beginning with a maximal definition containing several infinite attributes.

candidates.contextSummary: Swinburne points to the universe, simple comprehensible laws, conscious life, and evil as evidence relevant to identifying the most probable kind of first cause.

candidates.speaker: Richard Swinburne
candidates.proposition: Omnipotence is the greatest logically possible power, and because such a being knows value without conflicting desires, perfect goodness follows from omnipotence.
candidates.attributionBasis: Swinburne remains the uninterrupted speaker and explicitly develops consequences of his account of omnipotence through the conclusion about perfect goodness.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The argument supplies a positive coherence relation between two defining divine attributes while excluding pseudo-actions that are logically impossible from omnipotence.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: The opening discussion of whether maximal power is coherent and whether inability to perform impossible or evil acts limits God.

candidates.contextSummary: Swinburne defines omnipotence as power over every genuine action, argues that logical impossibilities describe no actions, and connects evaluative knowledge to unconflicted motivation.

candidates.speaker: Richard Swinburne
candidates.proposition: Literal omniscience conflicts with divine freedom, so an omnipotent God must know the past and logical possibilities but cannot know future free choices.
candidates.attributionBasis: The same marked Swinburne turn explicitly introduces omniscience as the remaining problem and continues until the moderator ends his allotted time.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This move preserves coherence by revising one of the motion's central divine attributes and specifying exactly which knowledge omnipotence requires or precludes.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: The maximal conception under discussion treats omniscience as knowledge of every truth, including future actions and choices.

candidates.contextSummary: Swinburne argues that advance knowledge of one's own acts removes freedom, while effective omnipotence still requires complete knowledge of the past and logical possibility.

candidates.speaker: Michael Huemer
candidates.proposition: All-powerfulness still requires infinite power because no finite amount is greatest, while even restricted omniscience entails infinite knowledge and intelligence.
candidates.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly returns the floor to Huemer, who thanks Richard and presents a continuous response until declaring that he has said enough.
candidates.loadBearingReason: Huemer directly restores his principal infinity objection against both Swinburne's greatest-possible-power account and his restriction of knowledge about future choices.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Swinburne's claims that God need only possess the greatest possible power and that divine knowledge may exclude future free choices.

candidates.contextSummary: Huemer compares power with unbounded velocity, argues there is no greatest finite quantity, and maintains that mathematical, past, and present facts already constitute infinite information.

candidates.speaker: Richard Swinburne
candidates.proposition: Power can coherently be maximal by covering the limited kinds of action, and Christian tradition permits a God who changes his mind rather than possessing exhaustive foreknowledge.
candidates.attributionBasis: A new marked Swinburne turn begins at event 619 and runs continuously through his conclusion about what Christian tradition requires.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The response attacks both pillars of Huemer's renewed objection by offering a non-quantitative account of maximal power and historical support for limited foreknowledge.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Huemer's renewed argument that maximal power must be quantitatively infinite and that omniscience necessarily involves infinite information.

candidates.contextSummary: Swinburne calls the infinity inference insufficient, appeals to limits on kinds of action, and cites scriptural and theological depictions of God regretting or changing judgments.

candidates.speaker: Michael Huemer
candidates.proposition: A limit on kinds of action does not limit the power required within a kind, and restricting foreknowledge still leaves infinitely many determinate truths to know and integrate.
candidates.attributionBasis: After the moderator initiates another round, Huemer begins a marked response and develops both points continuously until restating his impossibility conclusion.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move directly answers both components of Swinburne's defense and argues that neither action-kind limits nor open-future theology removes the relevant infinity.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Swinburne's appeal to finitely many kinds of action and to a theological tradition in which God may change his mind.

candidates.contextSummary: Huemer uses unlimited lifting and repeated lamp switching to distinguish power from action kinds, then argues that past, mathematical, and present truths still demand infinite cognition.

candidates.speaker: Richard Swinburne
candidates.proposition: Treating the ability to lift any weight as infinitely partitioned power imposes an artificial mathematical conception of infinity on an ordinary unified kind of action.
candidates.attributionBasis: The speaker change at event 772 follows Huemer's completed response, and the ensuing first-person objection matches Swinburne's previously stated position.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This is Swinburne's direct conceptual answer to Huemer's unlimited-lifting example, challenging the inference from unrestricted ability to an impossible quantitative magnitude.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Huemer's claim that being able to lift any weight entails possessing an actually infinite quantity of strength or power.

candidates.contextSummary: Swinburne argues that ordinary action descriptions should be understood naturally as unified abilities and not reconstructed through a mathematician's partition into infinitely many acts.

candidates.speaker: Michael Huemer
candidates.proposition: Zeno-style spatial division is an actual infinity because infinitely many spatial points and segments genuinely exist and are traversed, even though traversal needs no infinite power.
candidates.attributionBasis: Huemer begins a marked turn at event 841, distinguishes this point from his preceding strength clarification, and completes the Zeno argument before Swinburne replies.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The distinction is essential to Huemer's taxonomy of infinities because it defends actual extensive infinity while denying that every completed infinite structure requires infinite power.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Swinburne's contention that dividing an ordinary action into infinitely many parts is merely an artificial mathematical description.

candidates.contextSummary: Huemer distinguishes the quantitative strength example from spatial division and argues that motion really crosses infinitely many existing segments despite requiring only finite power.

candidates.speaker: Richard Swinburne
candidates.proposition: A one-to-one correlation with a familiar infinite series is insufficient by itself to establish that a divided action is truly infinite.
candidates.attributionBasis: The uninterrupted response follows Huemer's Zeno discussion and is identifiable as Swinburne's direct counterargument.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move directly contests whether infinite divisibility supplies the actual infinity underlying the challenge to divine power.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Huemer's claim that traversing infinitely many spatial segments constitutes an actual infinity.

candidates.contextSummary: After Huemer treats spatial traversal as crossing actually existing infinite segments, Swinburne disputes the inference from mathematical correspondence to genuine infinity.

candidates.speaker: Richard Swinburne
candidates.proposition: God's inability to perform bodily activities does not limit omnipotence because such activities are logically incompatible with God's necessarily bodiless nature.
candidates.attributionBasis: The sustained first-person exposition is explicitly introduced as Swinburne's new point and continues without a speaker change.
candidates.loadBearingReason: It supplies a general coherence defense of omnipotence by classifying apparent divine inabilities as logically impossible descriptions.
candidates.contextSummary: Swinburne distinguishes genuine powers from descriptions incompatible with a necessarily non-embodied God and applies the restriction to walking and marriage.

candidates.speaker: Richard Swinburne
candidates.proposition: A timeless conception of God would remove conflict between divine foreknowledge and power over the future, though Swinburne rejects that conception as unintelligible.
candidates.attributionBasis: The speaker continues Swinburne's closing exposition and explicitly contrasts medieval timelessness with his own temporal conception.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move identifies a major route to reconciling divine knowledge and power while explaining why the proposed defense is not adopted.
candidates.contextSummary: Swinburne notes that timeless divine action could align knowledge and control of the future, then explains his preference for an everlasting God in time.

candidates.speaker: Michael Huemer
candidates.proposition: A timeless God cannot change his mind because timelessness and possession of successive incompatible mental states would be contradictory attributes.
candidates.attributionBasis: The marked speaker transition begins Huemer's direct response to Swinburne's immediately preceding discussion of divine timelessness.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The reply presses an internal-coherence problem between a timeless divine nature and earlier claims involving changes of divine intention.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Swinburne's discussion of a timeless God alongside earlier claims that God can change his mind.

candidates.contextSummary: Huemer connects the proposed timeless conception to prior descriptions of divine mental change and argues that the combined attributes conflict.

candidates.speaker: Michael Huemer
candidates.proposition: The Christian incarnation appears to undermine the claim that God cannot walk or marry, since Jesus is held to be God and embodied.
candidates.attributionBasis: Huemer continues his turn and explicitly challenges Swinburne's examples by invoking traditional Christian claims about Jesus.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The objection tests the bodilessness defense of omnipotence against a central theistic doctrine that attributes embodiment to God.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Swinburne's claim that God necessarily lacks a body and therefore cannot walk or marry.

candidates.contextSummary: Huemer argues that divine embodiment in Jesus supplies an apparent counterexample to the asserted logical impossibility of bodily divine actions.

candidates.speaker: Richard Swinburne
candidates.proposition: The incarnation does not refute divine bodilessness because Christ has distinct divine and human natures, with bodily capacities belonging to the incarnate nature.
candidates.attributionBasis: A clear speaker transition introduces Swinburne's detailed answer using the traditional two-natures account of the incarnation.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The response preserves the bodilessness-based coherence defense by distinguishing the divine nature from Christ's embodied human nature.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Huemer's objection that Jesus walked and could have married despite being identified as God.

candidates.contextSummary: Swinburne invokes the traditional two-natures doctrine to separate what applies to God as divine from what applies to the incarnate Christ.

candidates.speaker: Richard Swinburne
candidates.proposition: Thomson's lamp should be analyzed through temporally extended events rather than instantaneous states, so its outcome must concern a final period of finite duration.
candidates.attributionBasis: Swinburne takes the floor after Huemer states the lamp paradox and develops a continuous response about events and periods.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move supplies Swinburne's principal metaphysical answer to a supertask intended to challenge coherent unlimited divine power.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Huemer's Thomson's-lamp challenge asking what state remains after infinitely many switches.

candidates.contextSummary: Swinburne denies that events occur at instants, treats instants as period boundaries, and redirects the lamp question toward an extended final period.

candidates.speaker: Michael Huemer
candidates.proposition: Thomson's lamp uses infinitely many nonzero-duration switchings within finite time and therefore does not depend on treating the final instant as an event.
candidates.attributionBasis: The marked transition returns to Huemer, who directly reformulates the lamp construction in response to Swinburne's period-based analysis.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The reply blocks the proposed dismissal of the supertask by showing that every component event may have positive temporal duration.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Swinburne's claim that the lamp puzzle improperly treats events as occurring at temporal instants.

candidates.contextSummary: Huemer grants that events require time but argues that shrinking positive intervals can contain infinitely many switchings before a finite deadline.

candidates.speaker: Michael Huemer
candidates.proposition: The lamp paradox requires neither a last switching nor zero-duration events because observers after the completed infinite sequence must still find the lamp on or off.
candidates.attributionBasis: The marked Huemer turn follows Swinburne's renewed period analysis and presents a complete counterexample with post-sequence observation.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The argument sharpens the supertask challenge by locating the disputed state during an ordinary positive-duration interval after all switchings.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Swinburne's insistence that only a final extended period, rather than an instantaneous state, is intelligible.

candidates.contextSummary: Huemer describes an infinite switching schedule ending before a later period of inactivity and asks what an observer during that later period would see.

candidates.speaker: Richard Swinburne
candidates.proposition: A finite interval cannot contain infinitely many periods of positive finite length, because any selected positive length permits only finitely many such periods.
candidates.attributionBasis: Following Huemer's question about infinite divisibility, Swinburne gives a sustained answer distinguishing abstract division from finite-length periods.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The response attacks the temporal premise needed for the proposed supertask and thereby supports the coherence of the restriction on divine action.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Huemer's contention that infinitely many extended switching periods can fit inside one finite interval.

candidates.contextSummary: Swinburne accepts division into periods in a qualified sense but denies that a bounded hour contains infinitely many positive finite-length periods.
